assertion_analysis.failure_condition: test_pointer_counter_sees_known_chain: the counter is asked to walk a fixed three-node parent array [1,2,2] from node 0 and must report depth 2. It fails if the counting loop stops one link early or late, or if pointer-doubling is introduced, because depth would then be 1 or 3 — so it is a positive control that the counter sees a known-present depth, and it is the assertion that guards the instrument's semantics rather than its non-invasiveness. test_instrumented_receipt_identity, assert depth["visits"] == vertex_flux.size: fails if the injected jax.debug.callback stops firing once per fori_loop visit (drops to 0), or if the injected _neighbour_roots is not the symbol the sweep resolves. Its two sides are independent — the count is produced by JAX executing the injected call site, the right side is the fixture's vertex count. It is not the self-comparison shape: reverting the fixture input cannot make it true. test_instrumented_receipt_identity, assert_sweep_identity(native, counted) (profile.py:163): compares the module's own _sweep_tree against a FunctionType copy whose only difference is an injected counted_roots, on the same sweep_args. Both sides take the test's input, so this is the shape the rule warns about only if the injected path is a pass-through; it is not — counted_roots calls roots_with_depth, which is a re-implementation of _neighbour_roots carrying a depth counter. It fails on any divergence of the injected path's output arrays, and the recorded negative control shows it reddening when the visit order is rotated by one position (main/negative-control.log, EXIT=1). test_instrumented_receipt_identity, assert_identity(reference, candidate) (profile.py:169): compares seven receipt fields of build_contour_tree against a replay whose _carrier_adjacency and _sweep_tree are replaced by the measured passes and the measured adjacency. It would fail if the recorded passes were fed to the wrong pass slot, if the injected adjacency omitted its third return, or if the instrumented arrays differed by one entry; it is a strict equality over 7 arrays, so it cannot be satisfied by construction. It lacks its own negative control — the recorded mutation fails earlier, at assert_sweep_identity, so the receipt-level equality is not itself shown reddening. That is a coverage gap about which claim has been falsified (non-invasiveness is shown; the replay-through-native-merge equality is only argued), not a self-comparison defect, and the doc states the control's failure point honestly ('on sweep output zero').
assertion_analysis.verdict: no assertion added by this run compares a value against the same variable the test supplied; the equivalence assertions compare two distinct implementations over a shared input, and both are falsifiable by a named change to the injected path.

findings.text: follow-on: check_text() is a third copy of the figure text-bound and text-overlap guard already present as a private helper in scripts/prototypes/xpoint_cell_owner/render.py:24-43 (_save) and scripts/prototypes/fine_grid_convergence/render.py:37-56 (_save). No owner module exists to extend — the search over nova/media/ and scripts/prototypes/support/ found no exported save-with-check, and the repo-side rule that one style module owns this function is not yet realised for prototype figures — so this is a duplication rather than a bypass of an existing entry point. It matters because the guard is the mechanism three separate nodes rely on to satisfy the artifact check, and a fourth copy will be written unless one is extracted. Does not hold the node: the landed figure was rendered and inspected and its guard passed.

follow-on: the projection's depth bound is the literal 14 (depth_bound, also inlined at lines 103 and 105) rather than derived from the largest vertex count in the ladder. For n=10,028 a union-by-rank forest bounds depth at floor(log2 n)=13, so 14 is correct for these four rungs and the doc states it correctly, but a re-run over a different ladder would silently reuse 14 and mis-state the projection, which is the receipt the repair node is meant to be measured against. Small and prototype-scoped; a max(ceil(log2(n))) over the ladder removes it.

The three claims I could check against files rather than prose all reconcile exactly: the doc's stage table equals main/rows/*.json stage_seconds, the round table equals main/rows/counts-*.json, and both fitted exponent tables equal summary.json's stages[].exponent and counts[].round_exponent to the printed precision (e.g. limited full build 1.4730, join round 1.5228, split round 1.5403). I also tested the estimate's model rather than taking its caveat on trust: fitting T = C*visits + B*rounds to the two no-append arms at 550 and 10,000 gives C about 23 us per visit against B about 15.8 us per round, whose 5000-cell prediction is 26.6 s against 27.9 s measured, so the per-visit term the projection omits is about 0.5 s and the estimate is sound rather than optimistic. The doc labels the projection an estimate and states that the <=10 s whole-read target is not yet met — the claim the brief asked for is the expected wall, and it is given as one.
item_verdicts.goal: The node goal is to measure why the contour-tree sweep makes the topology read's warm wall grow with exponent about 1.5, and to prescribe the repair. docs/research/contour-tree-sweep-profile.html delivers both halves: the stage walls and per-stage least-squares exponents at 550/2,000/5,000/10,000 cells for both carriers, and a prescription in section #repair naming union-by-rank with path compression over _sweep_tree (nova/equilibrium/contour_tree.py:243, parent update at :338) and bounded root queries replacing _neighbour_roots (:99-105), with batched arc emission replacing the per-visit _append_edges (:108). The 1.5 is attributed by measurement to the two parent-link sweeps, whose round counts fit 1.523/1.540 limited and 1.519/1.547 diverted while visits grow at exactly one per vertex. I checked the brief's leading candidate against the source: _neighbour_roots really is jax.lax.while_loop(unresolved, lambda roots: parents[roots], neighbours) — one parent link per iteration, not pointer doubling — and the visit loop really does chain parents (parents.at[neighbour_root].set(...vertex...) followed by parents.at[vertex].set(vertex)), so the doc's correction of the brief's 'pointer-doubling' premise is accurate and is itself part of the answer.
